title: Lineage
tagline: AI drafts a cited pharma dossier chapter, independently checks each citation, anchors on-chain.

prizes.placement: Best usage of Chainlink Confidential AI Attester
prizes.title: Best usage of Chainlink Confidential AI Attester

description:
Lineage is a provenance and verification layer for AI-assisted medical writing. Pharmaceutical value dossiers justify a drug's value to payers and regulators, and every claim has to trace back to real evidence. Bodies like NICE, the FDA, and ISPOR expect a clear audit trail and human oversight, but when a language model helps draft these documents it routinely invents or misattributes citations.
You give Lineage a confidential source document, a drug, and an indication. It drafts one targeted dossier chapter grounded in PubMed, with inline PMID citations. It then independently verifies each citation by pulling the real abstract and checking whether it actually supports the sentence, marking every citation as confirmed or flagged for human review. The chapter is drafted inside a confidential enclave, so the source document never touches a public model. The finished evidence bundle is hashed, stored on Walrus, and published under an ENS name, so anyone can re-verify the whole thing with no trust in us and no central server. It drafts a single chapter rather than a full dossier, and it is built as an augmentation tool with a human in the loop.
how_its_made:
The app is Next.js and TypeScript, deployed on Vercel. Three partner technologies each do a distinct job.

Chainlink Confidential AI Attester (dev preview) runs the drafting step inside an AWS Nitro enclave on model gemma4. We pass in both the fetched PubMed abstracts and the confidential source document, and the document never leaves the enclave or reaches a public LLM. The enclave returns signed digests over the content, request, and response, which we anchor as proof of how the chapter was produced.

PubMed E-utilities supply the abstracts. After drafting, a verifier re-checks every inline PMID against its real abstract using a verbatim-span grounding check and marks it confirmed or flagged. Early de-risk testing showed the model keeps the cited PMIDs in-set but misattributes about a third of them, which is exactly why the independent verifier is the headline feature and not an afterthought.

Walrus testnet stores the canonical evidence bundle as a blob over HTTP with no wallet, giving tamper-evident decentralized storage. ENS on Sepolia ties it together: a heor.dossier.latest text record on heor-prov.eth points to the Walrus blob, alongside agent version and capability records, so the name is a human-readable, mutable pointer to the latest evidence. Integrity is a SHA-256 over a canonical sorted-key JSON, recomputed in the browser on the Verify path so anyone can re-hash and compare to the on-chain value against a public Sepolia RPC, no keys required.

The notably hacky part was ENS registration. The ETHRegistrarController in the current ENS docs had been de-authorized in a Sepolia v2 redeploy, so commit() worked but register() kept reverting. We replayed ControllerAdded and ControllerRemoved events on-chain to find the live registrar, registered through that, and confirmed it still wires through the canonical registry so standard ENS resolution works.

That ENS registrar paragraph is worth keeping. It's the kind of "we actually dug into the chain" detail that reads well to a technical judge, and it's true.

Describe how AI tools were used:

This project was built largely with Claude, via Claude Code. As a non-developer with a health economics and genomics background, I designed the architecture, made the domain and HEOR decisions, and ran the de-risk testing, and used Claude to write and debug the implementation: the Next.js app, the PubMed integration, the citation verifier, the Walrus and ENS clients, and the SHA-256 provenance hashing. It was especially useful on an ENS edge case on Sepolia, where the documented registrar contract had been de-authorized in a v2 redeploy. Claude replayed on-chain controller events to find the live registrar so registration would go through.

AI is also part of the product at runtime. The dossier chapter is drafted by a model (gemma4) running inside the Chainlink Confidential AI enclave. The point of the project is to not trust that output blindly: an independent verifier re-checks every citation the model produces against the real PubMed abstract, because testing showed the model keeps cited PMIDs in-set but misattributes about a third of them. The model does the drafting, and the verification layer keeps a human in the loop.

That answer is honest and specific, which is exactly what they ask for, and it doubles as your story for the "explain how you used AI" question in judging.

One related reminder from the judging deck: they want your plan files added to the repo. If Claude Code left any plan or task files in the project, commit them so that requirement is covered.

Synthesized partner integrations with code links, ratings, and constructive feedback
Synthesized partner integrations with code links, ratings, and constructive feedback
Here's everything for the three partner forms. The "why applicable" lines are tightened to a sentence or two each, code links point at your actual lib files, and the ratings/feedback are honest (sponsors read these, and honest feedback reads better than flattery).

ENS — $20,000

Why applicable:

We use ENS as the human-readable, owned entry point to each evidence bundle. heor-prov.eth resolves through text records (heor.dossier.latest, plus agent version and capability records) to the current Walrus blob, so anyone can verify a dossier starting from just a name, with no central server in the loop.

Code link: https://github.com/vedantMahangade/heor-provenance/blob/main/src/lib/ens.ts

Ease (suggested 5/10): The read path via standard libraries is genuinely easy once a name resolves. The write/register path on Sepolia is what drags this down, for the reason below. Adjust if it felt worse to you.

Feedback:

On Sepolia, the ENS apps now register names into ENS v2, which is invisible to standard ensjs/viem reading the v1 registry, so a name can look unregistered (owner = zero) even though it exists. Worse, the ETHRegistrarController address in the current docs had been de-authorized in the v2 redeploy, so commit() succeeded but register() reverted at onlyController with no clear error. We only got unblocked by replaying ControllerAdded/ControllerRemoved events on-chain to find the live registrar. Please update the Sepolia docs with the current controller address, and clearly document the v1/v2 split and which registry the JS libraries read, this cost us hours.

Sui (Walrus) — $15,000

Why applicable:

We store the canonical evidence bundle as a Walrus blob for tamper-evident decentralized storage. The Verify flow fetches the bytes back from the Walrus aggregator and re-hashes them in the browser, so integrity is provable against the hash anchored on-chain. Walrus is the load-bearing storage layer of the whole provenance chain.

Code link: https://github.com/vedantMahangade/heor-provenance/blob/main/src/lib/walrus.ts

Ease (suggested 9/10): The keyless HTTP publisher/aggregator flow was the smoothest integration of the three, no wallet, no setup.

Feedback:

The HTTP publisher/aggregator with no wallet made this the easiest sponsor integration by far. Two things would help: document testnet blob persistence and epoch/expiry behavior more prominently (it's not obvious how long a stored blob survives), and publish any rate limits on the public endpoints. A tiny end-to-end "store, read back, re-hash to verify" snippet in the docs would have saved a step.

Chainlink — $14,000

Why applicable:

The dossier chapter is drafted inside the Chainlink Confidential AI enclave (AWS Nitro) on model gemma4, so the confidential source document is processed by an LLM without ever touching a public model. The enclave returns signed digests over content, request, and response, which we anchor as proof of how the chapter was produced.

Code link: https://github.com/vedantMahangade/heor-provenance/blob/main/src/lib/confidential.ts

Ease (suggested 6/10): The async submit-then-poll API shape is reasonable and the attestation digests are clean to consume. Dev-preview reliability is what holds the score back.

Feedback:

The async POST inference + poll pattern and the content/request/response digests were clear to work with. The main issue was reliability: the dev-preview endpoint went unresponsive for stretches with 240s+ timeouts, then recovered on retry, which makes live demos risky. A status/health signal and documented expected latency would help. Also, the note that inputs may be logged is easy to miss but critical, since the whole use case is confidential data. A prominent, explicit data-handling and retention statement would make it far easier to trust the enclave with real (not synthetic) documents.

Two quick notes on the code links: confirm those three file paths match your repo exactly (they're the lib modules you built). And if a field wants a specific line rather than a file, open the file on GitHub, click the line number, and use "Copy permalink", that produces a frozen #L link to the exact line, which is what sponsors prefer.
